title: Where We Begin
text:
Stress is a major issue for many students in academia. In small, manageable amounts, stress can actually help. This positive stress, called eustress, can keep us motivated and focused. But when stress builds too high, it puts students at a disadvantage, affecting their sleep, focus, health, and performance in school.


How stress builds and who get support?

title: Public Health Impact
text:
Stress plays a major role in how students succeed. It’s shaped by the professions they choose and by parental pressure that can push students toward degrees they may not want or may not be prepared for.
So what can we do as public health professionals? We propose a coordinated program at the local, state, and federal levels, built with a full group of stakeholders. The program would focus on improving mental health resources in both low-income and very wealthy communities, since students in both can experience high levels of stress. In wealthy communities, the stress often comes from outside pressure to achieve. In low-income communities, it often comes from a lack of resources. There, the program would add support like afterschool educational programs to ease the burden of school and remove obstacles to student success.
Next, we would bring together the people who shape a student’s experience: students themselves, families, schools and universities, campus counseling centers, community organizations, local health departments, and policymakers. Each level of the program would play a different role:

Local: Schools and campuses would make mental health resources easy to find, like the one-page Student Stress and Support Guide, and would partner with community organizations to offer afterschool and academic support. Family workshops would help parents talk with their children about what success really means, so high hopes don’t turn into harmful pressure.
State: States would fund school and campus counseling so students aren’t turned away by long wait times. States could also review licensing and bar admission questions that discourage future doctors and lawyers from seeking help.
Federal: Federal agencies would support research and data collection, like the Healthy Minds Study, and provide funding so that schools in every community, not just well-resourced ones, can offer mental health services.

Finally, we would measure whether the program works. Using survey data, we would track whether more students who are struggling get support, and whether barriers like lack of time and not knowing where to go become less common.
Stress among students is not just a personal problem. It is shaped by systems: the pressure of competitive professions, expectations at home, and policies that make asking for help feel risky. That is why public health matters here. By looking at the whole system, and not just the individual student, we can change the conditions that let stress build. When students can recognize stress, know where to turn, and feel safe asking for help, they are better able to succeed in school and in the careers they choose.

title: Stress Across the Academic Path
text: Stress doesn’t end with a bachelor’s degree. For many students, it changes shape. Graduate, medical, and law students face longer hours, high-stakes exams, debt, and intense competition. Professional students also face a pressure most undergraduates don’t: worrying that getting mental health care could affect their future license to practice due to social structures viewing them not fit for their role.

title: Stress Across the Academic Path
text:
Symptoms by path









What stands out:

College students overall report high symptom levels, though Healthy Minds data show depression and anxiety have declined each year since 2022.
Medical students show depressive symptoms in more than 1 in 4 students across 43 countries, well above the general adult population.
Law students stand out for anxiety: more than a third screened positive, and 14% screened in the severe range.
Graduate students vary widely by study. A large review puts depression and anxiety near 17% and 24%, while one well-known 2018 survey of mostly PhD students found about 4 in 10, though that survey was not a random sample.

title: Stress Across the Academic Path
text:
Who gets help
The bigger difference between paths may not be how many students struggle, but how many get help.









Medical students stand out: in the meta-analysis, only about 1 in 6 who screened positive for depression sought psychiatric treatment.

title: Stress Across the Academic Path
section: A pressure unique to professional students: licensure
text:
A pressure unique to professional students: licensure
Future doctors and lawyers must pass a licensing review before they can practice. Some of these reviews have asked about past mental health diagnoses or treatment. Students hear about these questions, and many decide it is safer not to get help.







Path
What the research found




Law (JD)
In the 2021 Survey of Law Student Well-Being, 44% of law students said they feared seeking help for a mental health issue because it could threaten their bar admission.


Medicine (MD)
At one U.S. medical school, 33% of students said licensing disclosure questions substantially discourage them from seeking treatment, and 91% were unsure or wrong about whether their state even asks.



This is where law and policy become a leverage point in the system:






That change is already happening. According to the AAMC, 43 medical licensing boards have removed questions about past mental health history and now ask only about current impairment. Several states, including Washington and Louisiana, have removed mental health questions from bar admission reviews.

title: Stress Across the Academic Path
section: Why this matters for the guide
text:
Why this matters for the guide
Morehouse School of Medicine trains future physicians and health professionals, so the barriers on this page apply directly to the students the guide serves. The Student Stress and Support Guide focuses on the earliest fix: helping students recognize stress and know where to go before fear and delay take over.

title: Family Expectations and the Pressure to Achieve
text:
Family involvement can be one of a student’s greatest strengths. Parents who encourage, guide, and believe in their children give them a reason to keep going. But when expectations feel excessive, the same involvement can become pressure. Students may feel they have to reach a certain degree, or a certain title, to make their family proud or to stay at the level their family already reached.
Research points to two different paths to that pressure:

title: Family Expectations and the Pressure to Achieve
text:
Path 1: Following in their footsteps
A Swiss-German study measured cortisol, the body’s stress hormone, stored in the hair of 71 first-semester college women. Students with at least one parent who had a university degree showed higher stress levels than students from non-academic households, even though the two groups didn’t differ in other respects. The researchers’ explanation: students from academic families may fear a drop in social status if they fail, while students without that legacy have less to lose. The authors call their findings preliminary, since the sample was small.
This pattern matters in professional fields, where many students follow a parent’s path:









Children of physicians are far more common in medical school than physicians are in the general workforce. Having a parent in the field can bring real advantages, like guidance and connections. It can also bring a quiet expectation that medicine is the “right” path.

title: Family Expectations and the Pressure to Achieve
section: Path 2: Reaching for what parents couldn’t
text:
Path 2: Reaching for what parents couldn’t
For many first-generation students, family is a central reason for pursuing a degree. Psychologist Rebecca Covarrubias and colleagues describe family achievement guilt: discomfort with one’s own college success when family members didn’t have the same opportunities. Students may feel guilty about having more freedom, learning things their family can’t share, or being away when the family is struggling.
That guilt has a cost. In one study, first-generation students reported significantly more depressive symptoms when their family achievement guilt was high, compared with students whose parents had attended college.
Support also matters in a specific way. First-generation students in one study received just as much moral support (“we’re proud of you”) from family as other students, but less academic support (help understanding how college works). Encouragement without a roadmap can leave students feeling they must succeed without knowing how.

title: Family Expectations and the Pressure to Achieve
text:
The pressure is rising
Psychologists Thomas Curran and Andrew Hill pooled 82 studies of about 24,000 college students in the U.S., Canada, and the U.K. They found that students’ perceptions of parental expectations and parental criticism increased steadily from 1989 to 2019. Those perceptions were strongly linked to socially prescribed perfectionism: the belief that others demand perfection from you. Perfectionism, in turn, contributes to depression and anxiety.

“Parental expectations have a high cost when they’re perceived as excessive.” — Thomas Curran

title: Family Expectations and the Pressure to Achieve
text:
How the system works






How to read this: a + means the two move in the same direction, and a − means they move in opposite directions. The map shows two loops:

The bar keeps rising: each achievement can raise the family’s expectations for the next one. A bachelor’s degree leads to “now medical school,” and the finish line keeps moving.
Struggling in silence: stress raises the fear of disappointing family. That fear makes asking for help feel like admitting failure, so stress keeps building.

The leverage point is the link between expectations and pressure. Open conversations with family about what success really means, and practical academic support (mentors, first-generation programs, advisors), can keep high hopes from turning into harmful pressure.

title: Family Expectations and the Pressure to Achieve
text:
What this means for students

Your family’s pride is not the same as their expectations. Many parents want their children to be happy and healthy first. Saying out loud what you’re feeling can change the conversation.
Find the roadmap, not just the encouragement. Advisors, mentors, and first-generation student programs can fill in what family may not know about college or professional school.
Getting help is part of succeeding. See the Student Stress and Support Guide for signs to watch for and where to go.

title: Student Stress and Support Guide
text:
ImportantIn crisis right now?



Call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or chat at 988lifeline.org. If you are in immediate danger, call 911.





1 · Recognize
Signs stress may be affecting your daily life

Trouble falling or staying asleep
Hard to focus in class or while studying
Feeling irritable, on edge, or overwhelmed most days
Headaches, stomachaches, or tension
Skipping meals, classes, or time with friends






2 · Cope
Things you can start today

Move your body, even a short walk
Try slow breathing or a few minutes of quiet
Pick your top priorities and let some things wait
Keep a steady sleep schedule
Reach out to people who help you feel better





3 · Find support
It may be time to talk to someone if you are struggling to cope, or your stress doesn’t go away or keeps getting in the way of school, sleep, or relationships. Asking for help early is a smart move, not a last resort.

Why students don’t get help









How to read this: a + means the two things move in the same direction, and a − means they move in opposite directions. Stress feeds two loops that make it grow on its own: falling behind adds to academic demands, and having less time pushes back getting help. The guide steps in at knowing where to go. That shortens the delay, so students reach support sooner and stress comes down.







This guide is for information only. It does not diagnose or treat any condition and is not a substitute for professional care. It does not collect any personal information.
